comparison: Perfect agreement on SMRT-seq analysis (C88-C100). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the findings that SMRT-seq showed high false positive rates and no differences between wild-type and TET mutants. Editor's statement that 'evidence supporting the claims is solid' encompasses this methodology.

Strong agreement on LC-MS/MS findings showing TET loss does not impact 6mA levels (C4, C29-C32, C61, C63, C66, C82-C83, C87). Both evaluations support the conclusion that contradicts prior literature. Editor explicitly states this 'challenges previous findings' and evidence is 'solid.' OpenEval also includes C6 and C71 in broader conclusion.

Agreement on 5mC and 5hmC measurements (C67-C70, C72). Both evaluations accept these findings as valid controls. Peer review implicitly supports through editor's statement about solid evidence; no reviewer questions these measurements.

Agreement on in vitro enzymatic assays (C101-C106). Both evaluations support the finding that TET oxidizes 5mC but not 6mA. Peer review accepts this as part of overall solid evidence. OpenEval notes C110 speculation about affinity; peer review includes broader claims C7, C33, C114, C129 about TET not functioning as 6mA demethylase.

Strong agreement on LC-MS/MS measurements under axenic conditions (C3, C28, C44-C46, C49). Both evaluations praise the axenic approach for controlling bacterial contamination (C42-C43). Peer review also includes C5, C47-C48 about tissue-specific findings. All three peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge this methodological strength.

Agreement on catalytic-dead mutant findings (C121-C127, C130). Both evaluations support the conclusion that TET's essential function is enzymatic-independent. Editor explicitly states study 'underlines the importance of TET non-enzymatic activity.' Peer review also includes broader claims C8-C9, C34, C117-C120 about the mutant generation and characterization.

Agreement on bacterial contamination validation (C75-C81). OpenEval also includes tissue-specific contamination findings (C47-C48, C78-C81). Peer reviewers emphasize the value of axenic approach, implicitly supporting these validation experiments. OpenEval notes some tension in interpretation about CNS contamination.

Agreement on axenic condition validation (C42-C43, C75-C77). Both evaluations support the PCR and genomic sequencing data demonstrating absence of bacterial contamination. Peer review emphasizes this as a key strength of the study.

Agreement on sequence analysis (C112-C114, with C113 shared). Both evaluations accept that Drosophila TET lacks key residues for 6mA binding. OpenEval notes this would be strengthened by structural modeling or mutagenesis. Peer review accepts this as supporting overall conclusion.

Agreement on catalytic-dead allele generation and characterization (C117-C120). OpenEval focuses on the CRISPR/Cas9 methodology and immunostaining validation. Peer review accepts this within broader evaluation of enzymatic-independent function (C8-C9, C34, C121-C127, C130).

Agreement on central conclusion that TET does not function as 6mA demethylase (C7, C33, C129). OpenEval includes broader set of claims (C6, C71-C72) representing convergent evidence. Peer review accepts this conclusion as supported by in vitro assays and overall evidence package. Both note this contradicts prior literature.

Agreement on TET's non-enzymatic function (C8-C9, C34). OpenEval notes mechanism is not investigated but claim is well-supported. Peer review explicitly endorses this conclusion through editor and Reviewer 3 statements about enzymatic activity-independent developmental role.

Partial agreement on interpretation of low 6mA levels (C128). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting speculation about whether low abundance precludes regulatory function. Peer review (R10) accepts the interpretation, with editor stating paper 'has potential to stimulate re-evaluations.' Reviewer 2 seeks additional characterization but doesn't challenge the interpretation.

Both address quantification of methylated adenines (C46). OpenEval supports the LC-MS/MS measurements. Peer Reviewer 2 accepts the quantification (~200-400 methylated adenines) but suggests additional characterization of genomic distribution, indicating interest in understanding these rare sites rather than questioning the measurement.

Overlap on central conclusion claims (C6, C71). OpenEval R8 addresses the overarching conclusion that TET doesn't regulate 6mA. Peer R2 focuses on LC-MS/MS evidence showing no TET impact on 6mA levels. Both support the same conclusion from complementary perspectives.

OpenEval evaluates the statistical analysis of apparent 6mA increase in one TET allele (C84-C86), concluding the p=0.075 result is not reproducible across alleles. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; this detailed statistical assessment appears unique to OpenEval.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN the reconciliation with prior literature (C107-C111), noting speculative claims about affinity and post-translational modifications lack direct experimental support. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific reconciliation attempts.

Peer Reviewer 2 suggests characterizing genomic distribution of the ~200-400 methylated adenines (C46), seeking insights into potential regulatory sites. This represents a request for additional analysis rather than questioning existing data. OpenEval R1 addresses C46 quantification but not the genomic distribution question.
